Yes, production of chemokines by perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) plays a significant role in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis. PVAT, which surrounds blood vessels, was once thought to be inert, but it is now recognized as an active participant in vascular health and disease. 

Chemokines produced by PVAT can attract inflammatory cells, such as macrophages and T cells, to the vascular wall, promoting the development of atherosclerotic lesions. These chemokines can also contribute to the recruitment of smooth muscle cells and the formation of foam cells, further exacerbating the atherosclerotic process.

Additionally, PVAT-derived chemokines can influence the function of endothelial cells, promoting endothelial dysfunction and enhancing the expression of adhesion molecules, which facilitates the recruitment of inflammatory cells to the vascular wall.

Overall, the production of chemokines by PVAT is a key mechanism by which perivascular adipose tissue contributes to the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis, highlighting the importance of considering the role of PVAT in the development and progression of cardiovascular disease.
